<reason>Side A built a coherent structural case (voluntary entry + real exit legitimizes institutional self-definition) and used solid secular analogies to shift the burden onto CON. But the debate turned on two exchanges CON won decisively. First, CON's "who volunteers for the burden" framing exposed that PRO's structural test measures family-level choice while the actual burden (sex-differentiated dress rules) lands on the individual—especially children—who never independently consented; PRO's answer ("the volunteer unit is the family") effectively conceded this rather than refuting it, and CON explicitly caught and exploited that concession in Rebuttal 2 and Closing. Second, CON's pressure question about secular sexed codes being dismantled forced PRO to retreat from the parity argument that anchored its opening ("law firm, restaurant, club"), admitting religious dress rules "were never claiming parity" — a shift CON correctly identified as revealing the real ask is an exemption from scrutiny, not equal treatment. PRO's closing reframing of CON's position as "banning religious identity" is a fair rhetorical move but doesn't repair the structural concession or the parity retreat. CON's Rebuttal 2 was clipped by the word-limit format note, which is a real execution cost, but the substance survived intact into the closing, so it only modestly tempers an otherwise clear CON advantage.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Pressure Question about the "who volunteers" gap, and PRO's answer conceding that "the volunteer unit is the family, not the girl" — which CON then weaponized in Rebuttal 2 and Closing as a self-defeating concession, alongside PRO's forced retreat from the parity analogy once CON noted secular sexed dress codes are being struck down as discriminatory.</best_rebuttal>
